candidates.label: Antonia Fortress, northwest corner of the Temple Mount
candidates.support: The first-century Jewish historian Josephus writes that "the tower of Antonia... was situated at the corner of two cloisters of the court of the temple; of that on the west, and that on the north," matching Wikidata's recorded coordinate for the site at the Temple Mount's northwest corner. The point is approximate to this corner of the Temple platform rather than to an excavated structure.

summary.text: The World English Bible's "barracks" in Acts, traditionally identified with the Antonia, is linked to that fortress by the International Standard Bible Encyclopedia, which places the Praetorium "in the neighborhood of the present Turkish barracks where once stood the Antonia and where was stationed a large garrison (compare Ac 21:32-35)." Herod the Great built the fortress at the Temple Mount's northwest corner; the first-century Jewish historian Josephus records that Herod "called" it "Antonia, in honor of" the Roman statesman Mark Antony. Acts describes Roman soldiers stationed there rushing down to rescue Paul from a crowd in the Temple, after which the commander allowed Paul to address the people from the barracks' stairs.

history.text: The first-century Jewish historian Josephus describes a Roman legion permanently stationed in this tower, which "went several ways among the cloisters, with their arms, on the Jewish festivals," to watch the crowds for unrest.

scripture.textWEB: Some shouted one thing and some another, among the crowd. When he couldn’t find out the truth because of the noise, he commanded him to be brought into the barracks.
As Paul was about to be brought into the barracks, he asked the commanding officer, “May I speak to you?” He said, “Do you know Greek?
the commanding officer commanded him to be brought into the barracks, ordering him to be examined by scourging, that he might know for what crime they shouted against him like that.

When a great argument arose, the commanding officer, fearing that Paul would be torn in pieces by them, commanded the soldiers to go down and take him by force from among them and bring him into the barracks.
But Paul’s sister’s son heard they were lying in wait, and he came and entered into the barracks and told Paul.
But on the next day they left the horsemen to go with him, and returned to the barracks.

politicalHistory.entity: Kingdom of Herod the Great (ruler: Herod the Great)
Ethnarchy of Judea, Samaria and Idumea (ruler: Herod Archelaus)
politicalHistory.note: The emperor Augustus did not grant Archelaus the royal title his father's will asked for, only "ethnarch." The first-century Jewish historian Josephus adds that Augustus took Gaza, Gadara and Hippos from Archelaus's share and added them to the province of Syria. The map doesn't draw Gaza's land separately, so it shows Gaza, and the coast south-west of it as far as Egypt, with this area.

politicalHistory.entity: Roman province of Judea (ruler: Prefects, e.g. Pontius Pilate)
politicalHistory.note: Luke links a census "when Quirinius was governor of Syria" to Jesus' birth, which Luke and Matthew place in Herod's days; the Jewish historian Josephus dates Quirinius's own census of Judea to this year. This map takes no position on how the accounts relate. The map shows Gaza and the coast south-west of it, as far as Egypt, with this area, since it doesn't draw them separately.
